issues.legal_issue: The High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction does not permit it to reappraise supported factual findings unless they are unsupported by evidence or perverse.
material_facts: The matter reached the High Court through a challenge under Articles 226 and 227 to concurrent factual findings of the lower courts.
The High Court set aside the finding that the tenant’s storage of articles had damaged the premises on the ground that there was no evidence of damage.
The record included the landlord’s pleaded allegation, his testimony that storing articles on the roof broke the tin sheets, and a photograph of the roof.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by setting aside the supported finding on a ground that overlooked evidence in the record.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction. A High Court may interfere with a lower court’s factual finding only where there is no evidence to support it or where it is perverse.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_factual_findings: A litigant challenges factual findings of a lower court or tribunal in a supervisory proceeding.
predicates.lower_finding_supported_by_evidence: The lower court’s finding has support in evidence contained in the record.
predicates.finding_not_perverse: The lower court’s finding is not perverse.

issues.definition: When factual findings supported by the record and not perverse are challenged in supervisory review, setting them aside is improper.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s imprudent use of leased property that causes damage constitutes a ground for eviction under the applicable rent-control law.
material_facts: The premises were leased for business and residential uses.
The tenant stored spare parts and old vehicles on the roof and in other areas of the premises.
The landlord testified that storing articles on the roof broke the tin sheets, and the record included a photograph of the roof.
The lower courts found that the tenant’s imprudent use had caused damage, and the Supreme Court held that the High Court had overlooked the evidence supporting that finding.
issues.conclusion: The finding of imprudent use causing damage supported eviction, and the eviction decree was restored on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides an eviction ground for an act contrary to Section 108(o) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Section 108(o) requires a lessee to use property as a person of ordinary prudence would use their own property and not to damage the leased building.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction under a rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_used_property_imprudently: The tenant used the leased property in a manner inconsistent with the care an ordinarily prudent person would exercise over their own property.
predicates.tenant_use_caused_property_damage: The tenant’s use of the property caused damage to the leased building.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding under rent-control law, a tenant’s imprudent use that causes damage establishes an eviction ground.

issues.legal_issue: The described departures from the leased uses did not establish a ground for eviction based on change of user.
material_facts: Two front rooms had been leased for a motorcycle workshop but were being used for residential purposes.
A rear room had been leased for residential purposes and was being used partly to store motorcycle spare parts.
The High Court set aside the lower courts’ finding of change of user, relying on earlier decisions, and the Supreme Court stated that those decisions supported the High Court’s view.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the High Court’s conclusion that the described uses did not establish the change-of-user ground for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: In considering whether a tenant’s different use of premises amounts to a change of user, the Court relied on Gurdial Batra v. Raj Kumar Jain, Sant Ram v. Rajinder Lal and Kisan Dayanu Mano v. Vithal Vishnu Mohandalo, and held that those decisions supported the High Court’s conclusion on the uses described in this case.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks a tenant’s eviction under a rent-control law.
predicates.premises_used_differently_from_leased_pu: The tenant puts the premises to a use different from the purpose for which they were leased.
predicates.use_departure_is_of_a_kind_treated_as_no: The departure in use is of a kind that the court treats, in light of the applicable precedents, as not amounting to a change of user.

issues.definition: A different use of leased premises does not establish an eviction ground for change of user when the court treats that kind of departure as not amounting to a change of user.
